cards.title: Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests

depth.text: a **Microsoft outage** meant a hotel missed an **email alert** about too much chlorine in its pool

At Phantasialand’s Hotel Ling Bao, a **faulty automatic dosing system** pumped too much chlorine into the pool. The sauna area's safety system had sent an **email alert**, but the Microsoft outage stopped emails arriving; **15 guests** reported health problems after visiting the pool.

cards.camps: Two camps: some treat the Microsoft outage as the reason the warning was missed; others say the hotel's safety setup should never have relied on email alone.

comments.text: I personally operate a fairly advanced closed-loop chlorination system, and this is beyond screwed up. These systems can easily fail, and they tend to fail in a way that causes them to measure low or zero chlorine and thus overdispense chlorine. More below on why. First, this means that an operator must always ensure safety, both against excessive chlorine and against insufficient chlorine. In a…
This is 100% fault of the hotel, not of Microsoft. It’s unacceptable that the communications regarding such a dangerous thing totally rely on email, without any backup or double check.

I'm not even going to read the article. If your hotel depends on some cloud service to prevent chlorine gas poisoning you're doing something terribly wrong. Full stop. I don't know anything about the laws in Germany but this is dangerously close to libel in the US. Disclaimer: I work in Azure, this is not a defense of the outage and I didn't read the submitted article.

Comments seem to be losing a fair bit in translation so rough translation: * 13 guests complaining about irritation of airways (+2 later) * 4 taken to hospital, 1 described as medium injury, rest discharged * Dual failure - dosing system had a defect (dosing too high) and the email of the monitoring failed (M365). Article sounds like it's two distinct systems. Overall the German text sounds a lot…
I know it’s fun to blame Microsoft for things, but that is a poor and dangerous design. Anything that could result in that sort of harm should have a more resilient and redundant architecture.

cards.title: Protomaps: Self-hosting map tiles has gotten cheap and easy

cards.title: Things That Turbo Pascal Is Smaller Than (2011)

depth.text: someone shows **Turbo Pascal**'s **compiler and editor** took less room than a **web page**
The entire Turbo Pascal 3.02 executable—the compiler and IDE—was **39,731 bytes**. It was smaller than the **yahoo.com home page**, listed at 219,583 bytes in the post's 2011 comparison.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see modern software as carrying avoidable overhead; others say comparisons across different eras and file types ignore too much context.

comments.text: Anders Heljsberg GOAT. Turbo Pascal, Delphi, C#, TypeScript, just a phenomenal career marked with better taste than any other language designer I can think of, certainly any designer whose work is so mainstream.

Or people trying radically different versions of efficiency and simplicity, like an OS that uses an existing battle-tested sandboxed execution environment like v8 for userspace safety/isolation. Fundamentally, many inefficiencies were justified…

glossary.automatic dosing system: Equipment that adds chemicals to the pool on its own, instead of someone pouring them in by hand.
glossary.closed-loop chlorination system: A pool setup that checks chlorine levels and adjusts how much chlorine it adds.
glossary.fail-safe: A safety setup meant to stop equipment from doing something dangerous when a fault happens.
glossary.reasoning effort: A setting for how much work a model spends figuring out an answer.
glossary.open weights: The model's learned settings are available for people to download and run themselves.
glossary.tokens per second: A measure of how quickly a model produces text.
glossary.PMTiles: A format for storing map tiles in one file that a website can fetch in pieces.
glossary.HTTP Range requests: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Range requests: a way to fetch just part of a file instead of downloading all of it.
glossary.CDN: Content Delivery Network: A network of servers that helps websites handle requests closer to their users.
glossary.storage bucket: An online place to keep files so a service can retrieve them.
glossary.XSS: Cross-site scripting: A flaw that can make a website run instructions supplied by someone visiting it.
glossary.iframe: A webpage shown inside another webpage.
glossary.trusted filter: A uBlock Origin rule treated as allowed to add JavaScript to pages.
glossary.UUID: Universally unique identifier: a label designed to identify one item without being confused with another.
glossary.URL shortener: A service that turns a long web address into a shorter one and sends visitors to the destination.
glossary.back-half: The part of a shortened web address after the slash; whoever claims it can choose where the link leads.
glossary.redirect: When one web address automatically sends you to another.
glossary.broken link hijacking: When someone takes over an old link and points it to a different page.
glossary.Unicode: A shared way to represent characters from writing systems around the world in files and software.
glossary.ligatures: A font feature that can combine neighboring letters into a single shape.
glossary.OCR: Optical character recognition: software that reads words from a picture or scanned page.
glossary.UX: User experience: how using a product feels and how easy it is to get things done.
glossary.compiler: A tool that turns code you write into a program a computer can run.
glossary.IDE: Integrated Development Environment: an app that brings coding and other development tools together.
glossary.executable: A file that runs as a program when opened.
glossary.minified: Code with extra spaces and other unneeded text removed to make it take up less room.
glossary.boilerplate code: Repeated setup code that has to appear in programs even though it isn't the part that makes each one different.
glossary.positional embedding: Information that helps a language model tell where a token sits in a sequence.
glossary.RoPE: Rotary Position Embedding: a method that turns pairs of numbers in a token’s attention calculations by an amount based on where the token sits.
glossary.attention: A way for each token to draw on information from other tokens in the same input.
glossary.query: A list of numbers that represents what a token is looking for from other tokens.
glossary.key: A list of numbers other tokens compare against to decide whether to use this token’s information.
glossary.causal mask: A rule that stops each token from looking at later tokens, while letting it use itself and earlier ones.
glossary.group representation: A way to describe transformations, such as shifting positions, as changes to numbers.
glossary.translation group: The collection of shifts that move something by different amounts, where shifts can be combined.
glossary.corvids: A bird group that includes crows, ravens, rooks, and scrub jays.
glossary.theory of mind: The ability to understand what another bird might be thinking and act accordingly.
glossary.feedback loop: The time between changing code and seeing whether it works.
glossary.El Niño: A natural warming pattern in the tropical Pacific that can shift weather in many places.
glossary.Emacs: A text editor with many ways to move around and change text.
glossary.EWW: Emacs Web Wowser: Emacs's built-in way to open and read web pages inside Emacs.
glossary.Searx: A search tool that combines results from other search engines.
glossary.reader mode: A browser view that strips away page extras so the text is easier to read.
glossary.static HTML: Web pages with fixed text and layout, rather than pages that change as you interact with them.
glossary.execution CEO: A leader who focuses on running the company's existing business smoothly rather than changing what it sells.
glossary.CUDA: Compute Unified Device Architecture: NVIDIA’s tools for using its graphics chips for computing work.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.business model: The way a company makes money: what it sells, to whom, and how.
glossary.cannibalize: When a company releases a new product that takes sales away from one it already makes.
glossary.off-session: Charging a customer's saved card when they aren't actively making a payment.
glossary.SetupIntents: A Stripe feature for saving a customer's payment details for a later charge.
glossary.payment processor: A service that handles card payments for a business.
glossary.merchant fraud: A seller taking money from a customer without their permission.
glossary.export controls: Rules that limit where a company can sell certain goods, often for security reasons.
glossary.circular deals: A set of deals in which companies trade with one another in a loop.
glossary.interim CEO: A temporary chief executive who runs a company until a longer-term choice is made.
glossary.ground stop: An order that pauses flights from taking off, while flights already in the air may be handled separately.
glossary.router: A power tool used to smooth or shape the edges of wood.
glossary.SOP: Standard Operating Procedure: agreed steps for handling a routine task.
glossary.packet storm: A burst of network messages that overwhelms the equipment trying to handle them.
glossary.multicast failure: A failure in a way of sending the same message to several places at once.
glossary.post-mortem: A review after an outage to work out what happened and how to avoid a repeat.
glossary.Lean: A computer program used to write mathematical proofs and check that their steps are correct.
glossary.formalization: Writing mathematics in a precise form that a computer can check.
glossary.Dunning-Kruger effect: A term for people sometimes failing to notice their own lack of skill or understanding.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.next-token prediction: Training an AI to guess what word or piece comes next in a sequence.
glossary.post-training: Extra training after a model's initial training that shapes how it responds.
glossary.agents: AI tools that can carry out tasks with some independence.
glossary.superintelligence: A hypothetical AI that would outperform people across a very wide range of tasks.
